Nipple trauma

Some randomized trials found short-term pain relief, including one sham-controlled study with lower pain through seven days. Findings for lesion healing are less consistent, and pooled reviews disagree.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Some randomized trials found short-term pain relief, including one sham-controlled study with lower pain through seven days. Findings for lesion healing are less consistent, and pooled reviews disagree.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact nipple-trauma category contains 12 publications: five completed randomized trials, one uncontrolled treatment study, one two-case series, two meta-analyses, and three protocols. One additional 50-woman randomized trial is mapped from the broader lactation category because it directly treated nipple pain and fissures. The protocol records are plans rather than outcome studies. The two meta-analyses overlap substantially in the trials they summarize, so they are not independent replications.

Human and clinical evidence

A double-blind randomized trial of 60 postpartum women found lower pain after one laser session than after sham treatment, beginning at 30 minutes and remaining lower at diary checks through seven days. Satisfaction did not differ, and the report identified no adverse effects (Gaitero et al. 2026).

A 58-participant feasibility trial found no statistically significant between-group differences in clinical outcomes; the authors emphasized that it was designed to test feasibility rather than efficacy (de Paula Leite et al. 2026). Earlier results are mixed. In a 59-woman trial, pain fell by two centimetres after the first of three daily treatments, whereas a separate single-session randomized trial found no pain reduction (Coca et al. 2016; Camargo et al. 2019).

A 16-woman pilot reported faster lesion healing and reduced pain, but baseline pain was higher in the treatment group, making the between-group change difficult to interpret (Chaves et al. 2012). In the mapped lactation trial, 25 women received PBM and 25 topical cream; pain scores improved in the PBM group over the four-week course, but this broader-category study does not remove the uncertainty in the nipple-specific trials (Elseody et al. 2024).

The 2025 meta-analysis limited to three randomized trials found no statistically clear pooled difference in pain. A second review included seven studies and reported less sucking pain and faster healing, but rated certainty low. Their different inclusion sets and overlapping primary studies explain why these summaries should not be counted as separate trials (Gaitero et al. 2025; Alves et al. 2025).

Animal evidence

No animal study of breastfeeding-related nipple trauma was identified.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No separate laboratory study of nipple trauma was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Protocols vary. The recent sham-controlled trial applied 2 J of red visible light at 660 nm to the nipple and 4 J of near-infrared light at 808 nm in a cross-pattern over the areola, once per breast. Older trials used red 660-nm laser or near-infrared LEDs around 860 nm, with different treatment counts and energy delivery. No head-to-head trial has established which wavelength, dose, timing, or schedule is best.

Interpretation

Short-term pain relief is supported by positive results in several trials, but the null trials and small samples prevent a firm estimate of how often or how long relief occurs. Evidence for healing is thinner and rests mainly on a small pilot and a review that combines studies with different methods. Pain relief and tissue closure should remain separate outcomes in future trials.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow-to-moderate for short-term pain relief with selected protocols Low for lesion healing
Publications and records13 relevant publications (12 exact-category and 1 mapped lactation RCT)

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Several randomized studies report less short-term pain, and one sham-controlled trial found lower pain through seven days after one treatment. Other trials were null, and two reviews reach different pooled conclusions while reusing many of the same small trials. Larger, independently replicated studies using common pain and healing measures would clarify the size and durability of benefit.
